big_picture:
This was a week when India and the rest of Asia went in opposite directions. Markets in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, full of companies that make chips for artificial intelligence, had their worst week since the Covid crash of March 2020. Investors there are worried that the huge spending on AI will not pay off.

India has few AI companies. Its market is made up mostly of banks, IT service firms and consumer companies. So global investors moving money out of AI-heavy markets have been putting some of it into India. Foreign investors have bought more Indian shares this November than in any month before, which has also helped the rupee climb to a seven-month high.

The risk is that the gains are narrow. Today a few big banks lifted the Sensex while most shares fell, and the fear gauge rose. If the global sell-off deepens, India may not stay apart for long. Markets are shut on Tuesday for Guru Nanak Jayanti.

stories.title: Sensex jumps 898 points to 83,919 and Nifty reclaims 25,800 as banks lead; both end at nine-month highs and post a fourth weekly gain
stories.tldr: The Sensex rose 897.96 points, or 1.08%, to 83,919.71 and the Nifty 50 rose 286.30 points, or 1.12%, to 25,800.60, their highest closes in about nine months. Banks and IT companies led the rise, even as Asian markets crashed. But more shares fell than rose, and smaller companies lagged.
stories.what_happened:
The Sensex closed 897.96 points, or 1.08%, higher at 83,919.71, and the Nifty 50 rose 286.30 points, or 1.12%, to 25,800.60, HDFC Sky reported. Both were their highest closes in about nine months, and both indices rose for a fourth week in a row.

The day did not start well. Shares opened lower after a heavy fall in the US and Asia, and the Sensex dropped to 82,403.37 in early trade, 5paisa reported, before buyers took over.

Banks did most of the lifting. The Nifty Bank index rose 2.49% and the Nifty Private Bank index about 3%. The Nifty IT index rose 1.30%, realty 1.55% and healthcare 0.8%. Media shares fell nearly 2%, and metal shares slipped 0.23%.

Apollo Hospitals, Axis Bank, Max Healthcare, Maruti Suzuki and HDFC Bank were the biggest Nifty gainers. Titan, Tata Steel, NTPC and Hindustan Unilever fell more than 1% each.

Beneath the surface the picture was weaker. The Nifty Midcap 100 rose 0.66%, but the Nifty Smallcap 100 fell 0.13%, Kotak Neo said. On the BSE, 2,456 shares fell and only 1,582 rose. The India VIX fear gauge jumped about 7.5%.
stories.simple_explanation:
The two main scoreboards of the Indian market, the Sensex and the Nifty, rose about 1% today. They are now at their highest level since February.

What makes today unusual is what happened elsewhere. Markets in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan fell 5% to 6%. India went the other way, mainly because big foreign investors kept buying Indian bank shares.

But it was not a good day for every share. More companies fell than rose. The big names went up, while many smaller ones went down. And the fear gauge rose, which means traders expect bigger swings ahead.
stories.analogy: Think of a class where the toppers score very high marks in a test but most of the other students score a little lower than last time. The class average goes up because the toppers count for a lot. That is what happened today: a few big banks pulled the Sensex up, while more than half the shares on the BSE actually fell.
stories.why:
Reports said steady buying by foreign investors, especially in bank shares, drove the rise. HDFC Sky said global funds were moving money out of AI-linked markets such as Taiwan and South Korea, which crashed this week, and into India, which has fewer AI companies. IT and auto shares also gained as investors moved away from AI-linked trades, it said.

Metal shares fell on weaker commodity prices and a stronger dollar, HDFC Sky said.

Nagaraj Shetti of HDFC Securities said the Nifty's underlying trend remained positive. He sees 25,500 as a support level on dips and said the index could move towards 26,000 and then 26,350 over the next one to two weeks. Kotak Neo said some fall from profit booking was possible.

implications.you: If you have a Nifty 50 index fund or a large-company SIP, it rose by about 1% today. A midcap fund rose less, and a smallcap fund may have slipped a little. One day's move does not change a long-term plan.
implications.markets: Investors are watching whether foreign buying continues and whether the global AI sell-off spreads. The rise in the VIX suggests traders expect bigger swings in the coming days.
implications.economy: A strong market and steady foreign money support the rupee and make it easier for companies to raise money. There is no direct effect on jobs or growth from one day's move.

stories.watch: Whether the Nifty holds above 25,500 next week, foreign investor flows, and whether the AI sell-off in the US and Asia deepens. Indian markets are shut on Tuesday 24 November for Guru Nanak Jayanti.

explainers.like12:
Imagine a scoreboard that adds up the share prices of 30 of India's biggest companies. That is the Sensex. Today its score went up by almost 900 points, to its highest level since February.

The strange part is that markets in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan had a terrible day. Those countries make lots of computer chips for artificial intelligence, and investors are worried that the AI boom has gone too far. So big investors from abroad took money out of those markets and put some of it into India, especially into big banks.

But not every share did well. More than half the shares on the BSE actually fell. The big banks just pulled the score up.
explainers.real_life:
Rohit, 29, is a sales manager in Jaipur earning ₹55,000 a month. He has two SIPs: ₹3,000 a month in a Nifty 50 index fund and ₹2,000 in a smallcap fund. Together they are worth about ₹1.5 lakh.

Today his index fund rose about 1%, a gain of roughly ₹900 on paper. His smallcap fund slipped slightly, because smaller companies fell even as the big ones rose. Overall he is a little ahead for the day.

He does not need to do anything. His SIPs keep buying every month whatever the market does. His salary account and FD are not affected by these swings.

stories.title: Asia has its worst week since 2020 as the AI sell-off deepens; Taiwan falls 6.2%, Korea 5.2% and Japan about 5%, while India rises
stories.tldr: Shares in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan crashed on Friday after another big fall on Wall Street, as investors doubted whether huge spending on artificial intelligence will pay off. Asia had its worst week since March 2020. India, which has few AI companies, went the other way.
stories.what_happened:
Taiwan's main index, the Taiex, closed about 6.2% lower on Friday, capping its worst week in decades, 24/7 Wall St reported. South Korea's Kospi fell about 5.2% and Japan's Nikkei 225 about 5%. An MSCI index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan had its worst week since March 2020, Reuters reported.

The selling followed a heavy fall in the US on Thursday. The S&P 500 fell 2.02%, its sixth losing day in a row, the Dow Jones dropped 1,101.11 points, or 2.19%, and the Nasdaq fell 2.25%. Nvidia lost 3.30%. Before Friday's US session, Nasdaq futures pointed to another fall.

India was a rare exception: the Sensex rose 1.08% on the same day.
stories.simple_explanation:
For the past few years, investors around the world poured money into companies linked to artificial intelligence: chip makers, big tech firms and companies building data centres. Their share prices went very high.

Now many investors are worried that these companies are spending far more on AI than they will earn back. So they are selling. Taiwan, South Korea and Japan are home to many chip makers, so their markets were hit hardest.

India has very few AI chip companies. Its biggest companies are banks, IT service firms and consumer companies. So some of the money leaving Asia's chip markets has been coming to India instead.
stories.analogy: Imagine a town where everyone rushed to open mobile phone shops because phones were selling so well. Then people start to worry there are too many shops and not enough buyers, and the shop owners rush to sell. A neighbouring town with grocery stores and clinics instead of phone shops is hardly touched, and may even get some of the business that moves away.
stories.why:
Reuters reports said the record Anthropic share sale this week failed to restore confidence in AI stocks after Nvidia's results, and investors are questioning whether AI spending will pay off. SoftBank, a big AI investor, was a major drag on Japan's market.

HDFC Sky said global funds were rotating out of AI-heavy markets and into India, which they see as less exposed to the AI trade. Minutes of the US Federal Reserve's last meeting, released this week, showed most officials expect to raise interest rates again, which also weighs on shares.

implications.you: If you have an international fund or a US tech fund, its value has likely fallen sharply this week. Most Indian equity funds hold few AI companies and have not been hit the same way so far.
implications.markets: India's decoupling from Asia has helped Indian shares this month, but analysts warn that a deeper global sell-off could drag all markets down together. Indian IT companies also depend on US clients' spending.
implications.economy: Little direct effect on India's economy for now. A long slump in US tech could, over time, slow orders for Indian IT services firms, which employ millions.

stories.watch: Whether US markets steady on Friday night India time, and whether the AI sell-off spreads to Indian IT shares and the wider market next week.

explainers.like12:
Imagine everyone in school suddenly wanted the same kind of trading card, so its price went up and up. Then some kids started to wonder if the cards were really worth that much. They all rushed to sell at once, and the price crashed.

Something like that is happening with companies that make computer chips for artificial intelligence. Their shares had become very expensive. This week investors got nervous and sold. Countries like Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, which have lots of these chip companies, saw their markets fall a lot.

India has very few such companies, so its market did not fall. Some investors even moved their money to India.
explainers.real_life:
Ananya, 34, is a software tester in Bengaluru earning ₹90,000 a month. Two years ago she started a ₹5,000 monthly SIP in an international fund that invests in big US tech companies, alongside ₹10,000 in Indian equity funds.

This week her international fund has fallen noticeably, because US tech shares like Nvidia have dropped. Her Indian funds are up, because Indian shares rose.

This is one reason many people spread their savings across different kinds of funds: when one falls, another may hold up. A week's fall does not change a long-term goal. Her salary and her company's work are not affected right away.

stories.title: Bank shares hit a record as foreign money pours in; IndusInd Bank jumps about 8.6% and tops ₹1,000, Axis Bank rises 4.7%
stories.tldr: The Nifty Bank index rose 2.49% and touched a new all-time high above 64,000, led by IndusInd Bank, Axis Bank and HDFC Bank. Foreign investors have bought more Indian shares this November than in any month before, and banks and finance companies have drawn the biggest share.
stories.what_happened:
The Nifty Bank index rose 2.49%, Kotak Neo reported, and hit a new high of 64,085 during the day, according to Business Standard.

IndusInd Bank rose about 8.6% to ₹1,003, HDFC Sky said. It was the first time the shares crossed ₹1,000 since July, Business Today reported, and they traded on unusually heavy volume. Axis Bank rose 4.72% to ₹1,446 and HDFC Bank 2.94% to ₹846. HDFC Sky said bank shares were up 5.9% this week.

Foreign portfolio investors have bought a record of more than ₹1 lakh crore of Indian shares so far in November, Business Standard reported. In the first half of the month they put ₹84,291 crore into Indian shares, the most ever in a fortnight, and banks and finance companies took more than half of that, Kotak Neo said, citing NSDL data. Exchange data showed foreign investors bought ₹7,411.41 crore, net, on Thursday, while domestic institutions sold ₹1,356.57 crore.

Separately, SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said the regulator would issue a consultation paper on easing some rules for foreign portfolio investors, Zee Business reported.
stories.simple_explanation:
Banks are the biggest group of companies in India's share market. When big foreign investors decide to put money into India, they often buy bank shares first, because large banks are easy to buy in big amounts and grow with the economy.

This month, foreign investors have bought more Indian shares than in any month before. A large part of that money has gone into banks. That pushed the Nifty Bank index to a new record today.

IndusInd Bank, which had a tough time over the past year, rose the most. Its share price crossed ₹1,000 for the first time since July.
stories.analogy: Think of a famous sweet shop during Diwali. When crowds of customers arrive at once, the most popular items, the kaju katli and the laddoos, sell out first and their price goes up. Indian bank shares are the most popular item for foreign investors, so when lots of foreign money arrives, banks feel it first.
stories.why:
Business Standard said strong buying by foreign portfolio investors drove the bank rally. Analysts at Motilal Oswal, quoted by Business Today on Thursday, expect bank earnings to recover over the next few years, led by private banks, and said stress in unsecured retail loans had largely eased.

IndusInd Bank's shares rose on a surge in trading volume, Business Standard reported. The bank had reported improving business, profits and loan quality in its September quarter, though its interest margins narrowed.

Business Standard also reported that analysts expect foreign flows to slow in December after this month's record buying, and that a correction is possible.

implications.you: If you hold a banking fund or a large-company fund, it has gained this month, since banks make up a big part of the Nifty. Bank share prices do not change the interest you earn on your savings account or FD, or your loan EMI.
implications.markets: Banks are now leading the market. If foreign buying slows in December, as some analysts expect, bank shares could be the first to feel it.
implications.economy: Strong bank share prices make it easier for banks to raise capital, which supports lending to people and businesses over time.

stories.watch: Foreign investor flow data each evening, and whether SEBI releases its consultation paper on foreign investor rules.

explainers.like12:
Banks keep people's money safe and lend money to people who want to buy houses, cars or start businesses. Many banks are also companies whose shares you can buy.

This month, lots of investors from other countries have decided India is a good place to put their money. They have bought more Indian shares than ever before in a single month. Their favourite choice has been big Indian banks.

When many people want to buy the same thing, its price goes up. So today the prices of bank shares reached their highest level ever. One bank, IndusInd Bank, went up by more than 8% in a single day.
explainers.real_life:
Suresh, 40, works in accounts at a textile firm in Surat, earning ₹70,000 a month. He has a home loan with an EMI of ₹22,000, an FD of ₹3 lakh, and a ₹4,000 monthly SIP in a large-company fund.

Today's record for bank shares helps his SIP a little, because banks make up a big part of the funds that track the Nifty.

But it does not change his home loan EMI or the interest on his FD. Those depend on the RBI's interest rate decisions and on his bank's own rates, not on its share price. A bank's share price rising simply means investors value the bank more.

stories.title: Apollo Hospitals jumps 5.3% to a record after Macquarie's double upgrade; Max Healthcare rises 3.9%
stories.tldr: Hospital shares rallied after the brokerage Macquarie turned strongly positive on them. Apollo Hospitals rose 5.29% to ₹9,200 and hit a record high during the day; Macquarie moved it from 'Underperform' to 'Outperform' and raised its target price to ₹10,500. Max Healthcare rose 3.88%.
stories.what_happened:
Apollo Hospitals was the best performer in the Nifty 50, rising 5.29%, or ₹462, to ₹9,200, HDFC Sky reported. During the day it touched a record high of ₹9,205, BW Businessworld said. Max Healthcare rose 3.88% to ₹1,081.

The brokerage Macquarie upgraded Apollo Hospitals straight from 'Underperform' to 'Outperform', a move known as a double upgrade. It raised its target price from ₹6,230 to ₹10,500, which BW Businessworld said implies about 20% upside from Thursday's close. Macquarie also upgraded Max Healthcare, reports said.

The Nifty Healthcare index rose 0.8%, HDFC Sky said.
stories.simple_explanation:
Big brokerage firms employ analysts who study companies and tell their clients whether they think a share is likely to do better or worse than the market.

Until today, Macquarie had been gloomy about Apollo Hospitals. Today it changed its mind completely, saying it now expects the share to do better than the market. It also said it thinks the share could reach ₹10,500, much higher than before.

When a well-known firm changes its view this sharply, many investors notice and buy, so the share price rises.
stories.analogy: Imagine a well-known food critic who once gave a restaurant a poor review. Today the same critic writes that the restaurant has improved a lot and is now one of the best in town. The next evening, there is a queue outside. The food did not change overnight, but the critic's opinion brought in new customers.
stories.why:
Macquarie said market expectations for Apollo's earnings had bottomed out and the share's valuation had become more reasonable, BW Businessworld reported. It said the early hit to profits from Apollo's expansion of hospital beds was already reflected in the share price, while the new capacity was filling up at a healthy pace.

Reports also linked the upgrade to the September quarter results, when Apollo's revenue and profit beat market estimates. HDFC Sky said healthcare shares also drew foreign investor interest.

implications.you: If you hold a healthcare or pharma fund, it may have gained today. A brokerage's view is an opinion, not a guarantee, and analysts often change their targets.
implications.markets: Hospital chains have become a popular group for investors who want businesses that are less tied to global trade or AI.
implications.economy: Growth of large private hospital chains adds beds and medical jobs, mainly in big cities.
implications.prices: No effect on hospital bills or medicine prices. A company's share price does not set what it charges patients.

stories.watch: Whether other brokerages follow Macquarie's lead, and how hospital companies' new beds fill up in the coming quarters.

explainers.like12:
Apollo Hospitals runs lots of big hospitals across India. Like many companies, it has shares that people can buy.

There are experts at big firms whose job is to study companies and tell investors what they think. One such firm, called Macquarie, used to think Apollo's shares would do worse than others. Today it said it had changed its mind: it now thinks Apollo's shares will do better than most, because its new hospital beds are filling up well.

When a famous expert changes their opinion like that, lots of people rush to buy. So Apollo's share price rose more than 5% and reached its highest level ever.
explainers.real_life:
Meena, 45, is a school teacher in Chennai earning ₹48,000 a month. Her family relies on a nearby private hospital for check-ups, and she has health insurance through her school.

Today's rise in Apollo Hospitals' shares does not change what her hospital charges or what her insurance covers. Hospital bills depend on the hospital's own rates and her policy, not on the company's share price.

If she holds a diversified equity fund, it may own a little Apollo, so it gained slightly today. A brokerage upgrade is one firm's opinion about the future. It is not a reason in itself for her to change anything.

stories.title: Rupee rises 62 paise to 92.67, a seven-month high, and breaks through 93 per dollar; gold falls about 3.4% and oil stays near $90
stories.tldr: The rupee rose for a fifth straight day, gaining 62 paise to 92.67 per dollar, its strongest close in about seven months, helped by foreign money and cheaper oil. Gold futures fell about 3.4% on MCX. Brent crude traded around $90 a barrel after swinging on Middle East tensions.
stories.what_happened:
The rupee closed 62 paise stronger at 92.67 per dollar, from 93.29 on Thursday, HDFC Sky reported. It was the rupee's fifth gain in a row and its strongest level in about seven months. A PTI report put the gain at 65 paise to 92.67 (provisional). The rupee crossed the 93 mark for the first time since April 20, and rose about 1.6% during the week.

On MCX, December gold futures were down 3.38% at ₹1,23,150 per 10 grams in the afternoon, Kotak Neo reported, and silver fell 3.89% to ₹1,51,350 per kg.

Brent crude for January was at $90.35 a barrel at about 3:36 pm India time, Kotak Neo said. It rose early in the day after reports of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a Houthi attack on Riyadh, then gave up those gains. HDFC Sky said Brent was down about 23% so far in November.
stories.simple_explanation:
The exchange rate tells you how many rupees you need to buy one US dollar. Today you needed 92.67 rupees, down from 93.29 yesterday. A smaller number means a stronger rupee.

Why is the rupee getting stronger? Foreign investors are bringing in lots of dollars to buy Indian shares, and they have to change those dollars into rupees. Oil has also become much cheaper this month, so India needs fewer dollars to pay for its oil imports.

Gold fell sharply today. Prices of gold and silver have been dropping for weeks.
stories.analogy: Think of the rupee and the dollar as two goods in a market. When many people arrive wanting to buy rupees, the rupee's price goes up. This month foreign investors have been queuing up to buy rupees so they can buy Indian shares. At the same time, India's oil companies need fewer dollars because oil is cheaper, so fewer people are selling rupees.
stories.why:
Forex dealers said continued buying by foreign investors, a weaker US dollar and lower crude oil prices supported the rupee, PTI reported. They said foreign investors were chasing returns in India as AI-related share rallies in the US, Taiwan and South Korea faded.

Oil swung on two opposite forces. Reports of tankers being hit in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on Saudi Arabia pushed prices up. But oil flows through the strait have returned close to their pre-war levels, and Brent was heading for a third weekly fall, reports said.

implications.you: A stronger rupee makes foreign travel, foreign education fees and imported gadgets a little cheaper in rupees. If you send money to family abroad, each dollar costs you less. If you receive money from abroad, you get slightly fewer rupees.
implications.markets: A steady rupee makes India more attractive to foreign investors, because their returns are not eaten away by a falling currency. Exporters such as IT firms earn slightly fewer rupees for each dollar.
implications.economy: Cheaper oil and a stronger rupee lower India's import bill and can help ease inflation, which was above the RBI's limit in October.
implications.prices: If oil stays near these levels, pressure on petrol, diesel and cooking gas prices eases, though retail fuel prices are set separately. Gold jewellery is cheaper than a few weeks ago.

stories.watch: Whether the rupee holds below 93 next week, and oil prices as tensions in the Gulf continue.

explainers.like12:
Every country has its own money. India has rupees, America has dollars. When Indians buy things from other countries, like oil, they usually pay in dollars. So the price of a dollar in rupees matters a lot.

Today one dollar cost about 92 rupees and 67 paise. Yesterday it cost about 93 rupees and 29 paise. So the rupee got stronger: you need fewer rupees to buy a dollar.

This happened because lots of people from abroad are bringing dollars to India to buy shares, and because oil has become cheaper. Gold also became cheaper today. Its price has been falling for a few weeks.
explainers.real_life:
Farhan, 38, is a pharmacist in Hyderabad earning ₹65,000 a month. His daughter is planning to study in the US next year, and he has been saving for her fees.

The rupee's rise this week helps him a little. A fee of $10,000 would cost about ₹9,26,700 at today's rate, compared with about ₹9,32,900 at Thursday's rate, a saving of roughly ₹6,000.

His wife has been thinking of buying gold for a family wedding. Gold prices have fallen a lot recently, so the same amount of gold costs less than it did a few weeks ago. Prices can swing either way, so neither of these is a reason to rush.

stories.title: Mahanadi Coalfields IPO subscribed 0.49 times on day two; big institutions bid fully but retail demand stays weak
stories.tldr: The IPO of Mahanadi Coalfields, a Coal India subsidiary, drew bids for about half the shares on offer by Friday evening, its second day. Large institutions bid for more than their share, but ordinary investors have bid for only a quarter of theirs. The issue closes on Monday, 23 November.
stories.what_happened:
Mahanadi Coalfields' IPO had been subscribed 0.49 times by 5:04 pm on Friday, its second day of bidding, HDFC Sky reported. That means investors had bid for about half the shares on offer.

Qualified institutional buyers had bid for 1.37 times their portion. Retail investors had bid for 0.25 times theirs, and non-institutional investors 0.18 times.

The price band is ₹129 to ₹136 a share. The issue opened on November 19 and closes on November 23. Shares are expected to be allotted on November 25 and listed on November 27, Upstox said. Part of the issue is reserved for Coal India's shareholders, Zee Business reported.
stories.simple_explanation:
Mahanadi Coalfields is a big coal mining company owned by Coal India, which in turn is mostly owned by the government. Through this IPO, some of its shares are being offered to the public for the first time.

People can apply for shares until Monday. So far, big investors like mutual funds and insurers have asked for more shares than are set aside for them. But ordinary people have asked for only about a quarter of the shares kept for them.

Many IPOs get most of their bids on the last day, so these numbers can still change a lot.
stories.analogy: Think of a new restaurant giving out a limited number of tickets for its opening dinner over five days. By the second day, the corporate bookings are full, but families have taken only a quarter of their tickets. The organisers still hope for a last-day rush, which often happens.
stories.why:
Goodreturns reported that retail demand had been weak and that the grey market premium, an unofficial sign of expected listing price, had dropped. An unofficial grey market tracker on Friday suggested a listing close to the issue price.

Coal companies face long-term questions as the world shifts to cleaner energy, though India still relies heavily on coal for electricity.

implications.you: If you hold Coal India shares, you may be able to apply under the shareholder quota. Applying for an IPO is a personal choice. A low subscription so far does not by itself mean the shares will do well or badly.
implications.markets: The response to this government-company IPO will be watched as a test of demand for state-run share sales.
implications.economy: Listing a state-run company lets the public own a slice of it and puts its finances under closer public scrutiny.
implications.prices: No effect on electricity or everyday prices.

explainers.like12:
Mahanadi Coalfields is a company that digs coal out of the ground, mostly in Odisha. That coal is burned in power plants to make electricity for homes and factories.

The company is owned by Coal India, which is owned mostly by the government. Now it is selling some of its shares to the public for the first time. This is called an IPO.

People can ask to buy shares until Monday. So far, big investors have asked for all the shares kept for them. But ordinary people have asked for only about one in every four shares kept for them. Often lots of people apply on the last day, so we will know the full picture on Monday.
explainers.real_life:
Pooja, 27, is a nurse in Bhubaneswar earning ₹40,000 a month. She opened a demat account last year and holds a few Coal India shares. Her colleague asked whether she plans to apply for the Mahanadi Coalfields IPO.

At the top of the price band, ₹136 a share, the money she would need depends on the minimum lot size. Because she holds Coal India shares, she may be able to apply in the shareholder quota as well as the retail one.

Whether to apply is her own decision. She can read the company's offer document, think about whether she can afford to lock up the money, and remember that IPO shares can list below the issue price as well as above it.

concept.explanation:
Most of the time, stock markets around the world move in the same direction. The same big global funds invest in many countries, and they react to the same news, such as US interest rates or oil prices. So when Wall Street has a bad night, Asian markets, including India, often fall the next morning.

Decoupling is when one market breaks away from that pattern and moves on its own. It usually happens because that market is built differently. If the worry is about one industry, a market with little of that industry can escape the damage, and may even attract money leaving the others.

Decoupling is often temporary. If a global sell-off turns into a wider panic, investors may sell everything, and markets start moving together again. So analysts watch closely to see whether a decoupling lasts.
concept.example: On Friday, Taiwan's market fell about 6.2%, South Korea's 5.2% and Japan's about 5% in a sell-off of AI and chip shares. On the same day, India's Sensex rose 1.08%. HDFC Sky said global funds were moving money out of AI-heavy markets and into India, which has few AI companies.
concept.takeaway: Decoupling means one market goes its own way while others move together, usually because it is made up of different kinds of companies. It can last days or months, but rarely for ever.

quiz.why: The sell-off hit markets full of AI and chip companies. India's market is made up mostly of banks, IT services and consumer firms, and foreign investors kept buying.

quiz.q: The rupee moved from 93.29 to 92.67 per dollar. What does that mean?
